newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-GATTING BRIDGES THE GAP AS LIFE BEGINS AT 40.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-GATTING BRIDGES THE GAP AS LIFE BEGINS AT 40.

text.p: Amid the euphoria of England's nine wicket win over Australia in the first test at Edgbaston last weekend, one milestone slipped by without murmur -- Mike Gatting turned 40 on Friday.

It might not seem greatly significant in itself but Gatting, capped 79 times and still playing county cricket for Middlesex, represents a bridge between this England team and the last one to win the Ashes, in Australia, in 1986/87.

Then, all bulldog bark, he was the captain. Now, with the beard a touch greyer and the girth slightly fuller, he is a selector and nothing pleased him more last Thursday than to see England's bowlers skittle Australia for 118 on the first morning of the test.
"You won't get many better days than that," he says enthusiastically. "It was unbelievable really.
"When we took over, we wanted people to be proud of playing for England and go out there and show it. It's been noticeable that the right spirit and the right attitude is there."

He plays down his role as a selector but it is evident that the background role suits him well. Indeed, his recent decision to step down from the Middlesex captaincy after 14 years at the helm, suggests that one of English cricket's elder statesmen is preparing to shuffle off the playing stage altogether.
"As soon as I stop enjoying it then I won't play any more. Obviously, if I'm not playing well I won't be enjoying it, so i'll retire. But I don't think I'll go on after next year."

Indeed, his current contract runs through to the end of 1998 but it is a widely known fact that Gatting has set his sights on reaching 100 first-class centuries, a landmark achieved previously by 23 batsmen including his England contemporary and fellow selector Graham Gooch. If he has not made it by then, he may be tempted to give it one last shot.
At the moment he has 92 centuries to his name. It should be 93 but as England were taking a firm grip on the first test, he fell six runs short of the mark against Leicestershire at Lord's.
At least, however, it marked a genuine return to form after handing over the captaincy to Mark Ramprakash.

Gatting had not scored more than 34 in the county championship before relinquishing the role but two days later he made a century against Northamptonshire and followed that with his 94 against Leicestershire.
"Not doing the captaincy has helped," he says. "I can relax a bit now and just get on and play which is good.
"But I do still find myself thinking about field placing and that sort of thing and then I think 'Christ, why should I be worrying about it?'"
Ever the complete professional, Gatting is making a conscious effort to drift into the background and not bombard Ramprakash with advice.
"Ramps is going to have a lot of people shouting in his ear so I try and say as little as possible. If he really wants to ask, I'll give an opinion but it's very important that I stay quiet."
Gatting staying quiet? Now that is something English cricket hasn't witnessed in a long time.
